title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Mediastinal trauma encompasses a spectrum of life-threatening injuries to vital thoracic structures, including the heart, great vessels, trachea, esophagus, and thoracic duct. These injuries often result from high-impact mechanisms such as motor vehicle collisions, penetrating trauma, or severe deceleration. Due to the mediastinum’s complex anatomy and its frequent association with polytrauma, early recognition and rapid stabilization are crucial for optimal outcomes. Diagnosis relies on a combination of hemodynamic assessment, imaging, and surgical exploration when instability or persistent bleeding is present. Timely multidisciplinary management is critical to preventing complications such as cardiac tamponade, great vessel rupture, and mediastinitis.

content: Clinicians participating in this course can expect to gain a deeper understanding of the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management of mediastinal trauma, including the interpretation of imaging studies, informed surgical decision-making, and the provision of postoperative care. title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Introduction
content: Mediastinal trauma refers to an injury involving the central compartment of the thoracic cavity, which houses several critical anatomical structures. The mediastinum is often categorized into 3 clinically relevant sections: anterior, middle, and posterior. The anterior mediastinum contains the thymus and the internal thoracic branches, surrounded by connective and adipose tissue that cushions the vital cardiac structures underlying it in the middle mediastinum. The middle contains the pericardium, heart, ascending aorta, and great vessels, and trachea/main bronchi. The posterior mediastinum contains the esophagus, descending aorta, intrathoracic vena cava, thoracic duct, and azygos/hemiazygos veins. In trauma surgery, particular attention to mediastinal injury should be paid for penetrating injuries to the “cardiac box,” whose anatomical borders are the midclavicular lines laterally, the sternal notch superiorly, and the tip of the xiphoid inferiorly.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Introduction
content: Given the importance of these structures and their proximity, traumatic injury to this area can be immediately life-threatening. A large portion of individuals with trauma who experience mediastinal injuries may not make it to the hospital alive, and survival is contingent upon minimizing the time from injury to treatment. Historically, mandatory operative exploration was the primary practice. However, all patients should be treated according to the principles of Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS). With advancements in modern diagnostic and radiologic modalities (such as combined arteriography, esophagoscopy, bronchoscopy, and echocardiography), unnecessary explorations can now be avoided.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Etiology
content: The most common cause of blunt thoracic trauma in the United States (US) is motor vehicle collisions. Factors associated with mediastinal trauma in motor vehicle accidents include high speeds, not wearing a seatbelt, extensive motor vehicle damage, and the presence of steering wheel deformities. Proposed mechanisms include rapid deceleration, shearing forces, osseous pinch or injury from a sternal or rib fracture, and a sudden increase in hydrostatic forces or water-hammer phenomenon (thump effect). Penetrating thoracic trauma in the US most often occurs from gunshots and stab wounds. Other less common causes of penetrating thoracic injury include impalement by objects as a result of industrial accidents, falls, collisions, blast injuries, and military devices. [1] [2]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Epidemiology
content: While the incidence of isolated mediastinal trauma is unknown, chest trauma is the third most common type of trauma in the US after head and extremity trauma. About 25% of traumatic deaths in the US are related to thoracic injuries. [3] [4] The incidence of penetrating thoracic trauma varies greatly by geographic distribution. In Europe, for example, the incidence of thoracic trauma is estimated as low as 4%; however, in war-ridden regions, up to 95% of military deaths may be from penetrating thoracic trauma. [5] [6] In the US, thoracic gunshot wounds make up about 10% of major traumas, while stab wounds to the thorax make up about 9.5%. [7] [8]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- History and Physical
content: Care of the patient with mediastinal trauma typically begins in the trauma bay, guided by ATLS principles. Initial management focuses on rapid identification of life-threatening conditions such as hypovolemic shock from hemorrhage or obstructive shock from cardiac tamponade. First responders often provide invaluable information about the mechanism of injury, which can guide early suspicion for mediastinal involvement. For instance, penetrating wounds at the root of the neck should raise concern for great vessel injury. At the same time, high-velocity blunt trauma, such as from moving vehicle collisions or falls from height, can result in cardiac, tracheobronchial, or aortic disruption. After the primary survey and stabilization of airway, breathing, and circulation, a secondary survey should be performed to identify additional injuries through a meticulous head-to-toe examination. Even patients who initially present hemodynamically stable require close monitoring for early signs of decompensation, as deterioration may signal evolving tamponade, vascular rupture, or mediastinal hematoma expansion.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- History and Physical
content: The history and physical examination play a crucial role in the early recognition of conditions. Patients may report chest or retrosternal pain, dyspnea, hoarseness (suggesting recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement), hemoptysis, or dysphagia/odynophagia due to tracheobronchial or esophageal injury. On physical examination, findings may include subcutaneous emphysema, a Hamman sign (a crunching sound synchronous with the heartbeat), hypotension, jugular venous distension, or diminished heart sounds, all of which are consistent with cardiac tamponade. [9] Asymmetrical upper extremity blood pressures or pulses, a thrill or bruit at the thoracic outlet, or an expanding suprasternal or intrascapular hematoma may indicate great vessel injury. Inspection should also assess for seatbelt marks, sternal deformities, and tracheal deviation. A focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) exam can rapidly detect pericardial fluid, while chest radiography may reveal a widened mediastinum or pneumomediastinum. Together, a well-structured ATLS-guided assessment, combined with early recognition of these key clinical findings, is essential for promptly diagnosing mediastinal trauma and determining the need for surgical exploration or advanced imaging.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Evaluation
content: All patients with trauma involving mediastinal injury should undergo a standard laboratory panel, including a complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation studies, venous blood gas analysis, and serum lactate levels to assess tissue perfusion and metabolic status. When blunt cardiac injury is suspected, electrocardiography (ECG) and cardiac biomarkers such as troponin should be obtained. A normal ECG and negative troponins effectively rule out significant blunt cardiac injury. In contrast, abnormal results warrant a formal echocardiogram to evaluate for wall motion abnormalities, pericardial effusion, or tamponade physiology. [10] [11] [12]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Evaluation -- Radiographic Evaluation
content: Imaging is fundamental to the evaluation of mediastinal trauma. A chest x-ray (CXR) and extended focused assessment with sonography in trauma (eFAST) are standard adjuncts during the secondary survey. Supine CXR, as recommended by ATLS, may reveal mediastinal widening (>8 cm supine or >6 cm upright), pneumomediastinum, or obscuration of the aortic knob—findings that suggest possible aortic, great vessel, or pericardial injury. However, CXR lacks sensitivity for major vascular injury and should prompt further imaging when suspicion remains high. [13] The eFAST exam provides rapid bedside detection of pericardial fluid with excellent sensitivity and specificity. Still, it can yield false negatives if blood decompresses into the pleural cavity through a pericardial tear. In such cases, a formal echocardiogram offers a more comprehensive evaluation of pericardial and cardiac structures. [2]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Evaluation -- Radiographic Evaluation
content: In hemodynamically stable individuals, contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) angiography (CTA) is the gold standard for evaluating mediastinal trauma. CT delineates injuries to the aorta, pulmonary arteries, tracheobronchial tree, esophagus, and heart, and can define the trajectory of penetrating objects, detect hematomas, and identify air or fluid collections. Oral contrast can highlight esophageal perforations, while intravenous (IV) contrast enhances visualization of vascular injury, such as aortic transection or pseudoaneurysm. [14] [15] ECG-gated CT can further enhance the visualization of dynamic mediastinal structures (eg, coronary arteries, aortic root, cardiac chambers) and reduce motion artifacts. [1] In selected cases, catheter angiography remains valuable for diagnostic clarification and therapeutic intervention, such as endovascular repair of vascular injuries. However, false negatives can occur if injuries are temporarily sealed or small extravasations are obscured. [1]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Evaluation -- Endoscopic Evaluation
content: When imaging or symptoms suggest aerodigestive tract injury, bronchoscopy and esophagoscopy are indicated. Flexible bronchoscopy allows direct visualization of the tracheobronchial tree to identify tears, bleeding, or air leaks, while esophagoscopy can confirm or exclude esophageal perforation. [16] A double-contrast esophagram may also be used as an adjunct for detecting small or contained esophageal leaks.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Evaluation -- Endoscopic Evaluation
content: In summary, the evaluation of mediastinal trauma combines structured ATLS-guided resuscitation, targeted laboratory and imaging studies, and selective endoscopic assessment. Collaboration among trauma surgeons, thoracic surgeons, radiologists, emergency clinicians, anesthesiologists, and critical care teams is crucial for accurately interpreting findings and determining whether operative intervention or conservative management is appropriate. Early recognition and multidisciplinary coordination are essential to improve survival and minimize complications in patients with mediastinal trauma.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management
content: Clinically stable individuals, without evidence of injury after appropriate evaluation, may be discharged. Patients with signs or symptoms of blunt cardiac injury should be admitted to the hospital with continuous hemodynamic monitoring for a minimum of 24 hours. Those who are hemodynamically unstable in the trauma bay require immediate damage control resuscitation (DCR). DCR aims to prevent or arrest the lethal triad of acidosis, hypothermia, and coagulopathy. In this population, DCR includes restrictive crystalloid administration with early and balanced blood product therapy and permissive hypotension. Permissive hypotension in this context refers to targeting a systolic blood pressure of 80 to 90 mm Hg or a mean arterial pressure of 50 mm Hg until surgical control of bleeding is achieved. Nonjudicious fluid administration before hemostasis may lead to further bleeding through hydraulic acceleration of hemorrhage, dissolution of soft clots by increasing intravascular pressure, and dilution of clotting factors. [4]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management
content: Resuscitative or emergency department (ED) thoracotomy is a potentially lifesaving maneuver for trauma patients in cardiac arrest. ED thoracotomy allows for DCR through decompression of pericardial tamponade and arrest of bleeding from cardiac, lung, and great vessel injury. Maneuvers may include cross-clamping the aorta, open cardiac massage, and defibrillation with internal paddles, with the hope of improving cardiac output and increasing perfusion of the heart and brain.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management
content: Survival from ED thoracotomy varies greatly depending on the location and mechanism of injury, and whether the patient had vital signs upon presentation. Patients with isolated stab wounds can have a survival rate as high as 16.8%, while those with gunshot wounds have a 4.3%. Survival of ED thoracotomy from blunt injury is poor at only 1.4%. Patients with thoracic injuries have the highest survival rate from ED thoracotomy at 10.7%. Those with abdominal injuries have a survival rate of 4.5%, while those with multiple injuries have a dismal survival rate of 0.7%. [17] [18]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management
content: The appropriate indications for resuscitative thoracotomy continue to be debated. Several practice guidelines have been established by various organizations, including the American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (ACS-COT), the Western Trauma Association (WTA), and the Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma. [19] [20] [21] The practice management guidelines published by the WTA give the following indications for resuscitative thoracotomy: Blunt trauma patients with less than 10 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) Penetrating torso trauma patients with less than 15 minutes of CPR Patients with penetrating trauma to the neck or extremity, with less than 5 minutes of prehospital CPR Patients in profound refractory shock Patients with penetrating mediastinal trauma have the highest survival rate of patients receiving resuscitative thoracotomy. [22]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Thoracotomy Technique
content: The standard incision for a left anterolateral thoracotomy (ED thoracotomy) extends from the costal margin to the midaxillary line in the fourth or fifth intercostal space through the skin, subcutaneous tissue, pectoralis major, and intercostals down to the pleura, with care to avoid injury to the internal mammary and intercostal vessels. Mayo scissors are then used to divide the remaining tissue and pleura, preventing injury to the underlying lung. A large self-retaining retractor, such as a Finochietto, is used to expose the left thoracic cavity and inspect for overt signs of hemorrhage. If no obvious source of bleeding is found, the pericardial sac can be opened to facilitate further exploration. This involves grasping the pericardium with toothed forceps and making a vertical incision, being careful to preserve the phrenic nerve. Once opened, cardiac tamponade is usually relieved. Opening the pericardial sac also allows for the visualization and repair of any cardiac injuries, as well as cardiac massage and intracardiac epinephrine injection.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Thoracotomy Technique
content: After sharply dividing the inferior pulmonary ligament, the lungs can be swept anteromedially to expose the posterior mediastinum, allowing for cross-clamping of the descending aorta. If required, additional exposure may be obtained by transecting the sternum transversely with a Lebske knife or trauma shears and extending the incision into a clamshell thoracotomy to examine the right thoracic cavity. If a great vessel is injured, temporary control of bleeding can be obtained with direct digital pressure, occlusion with a Satinsky clamp, or even with balloon tamponade with a Foley catheter until definitive operative management. Venous injury can be addressed with a side-biting clamp and simple lateral repair. If this is not possible, division and ligation can be done without any hesitation. If necessary and potentially lifesaving, an injured artery can also be ligated, accepting the risk of stroke. Patients who regain vital signs should be taken to surgery expeditiously for definitive management. [23] [24]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Thoracotomy Technique
content: Median sternotomy is the preferred exposure for cardiac injury or proximal great vessel/superior mediastinal injury. Posterolateral thoracotomy for aorta/posterior mediastinal structures may be preferred depending on the case. Thought should be given towards having a cell-saver available in cases of possible significant volume blood loss, and/or a bypass available for cardiac and aortic injuries. Shunts may also be considered for vascular injury.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Cardiac Tamponade
content: The pericardial sac is a fibrous, non-distensible structure that usually contains up to 30 mL of serous fluid, which serves as a lubricant between the visceral and parietal pericardium. Cardiac tamponade results when pericardial pressure exceeds intracardiac filling pressure, leading to impaired diastolic filling and obstructive shock. As little as 60 to 150 mL of fluid can cause hemodynamic collapse, depending on the rate of accumulation. Classic findings include Beck triad (hypotension, jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds), pulsus paradoxus (>10 mm Hg drop in systolic blood pressure with inspiration), and Kussmaul sign (rise in jugular venous pressure with inspiration). However, these may be absent in the acute trauma setting.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Cardiac Tamponade
content: In those with trauma with equivocal imaging or inconclusive eFAST findings, a subxiphoid pericardial window remains a critical diagnostic and therapeutic maneuver. The procedure is performed by making a 5- to 8-cm midline incision over the xiphoid process. The linea alba is divided, and the xiphoid process is excised to expose the retrosternal space. Blunt finger dissection is carried cephalad, and the diaphragmatic pericardium is exposed and elevated with 2 clamps. After ensuring meticulous hemostasis to prevent false-positive results, the pericardium is incised between the clamps. The presence of blood or clot confirms tamponade or cardiac injury, prompting immediate conversion to median sternotomy for definitive exposure and repair. A negative window may be closed after confirming hemostasis, though some surgeons advocate leaving a drain in situ if the patient is unstable or suspicion remains high.
contents: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Cardiac Tamponade. In those with trauma with equivocal imaging or inconclusive eFAST findings, a subxiphoid pericardial window remains a critical diagnostic and therapeutic maneuver. The procedure is performed by making a 5- to 8-cm midline incision over the xiphoid process. The linea alba is divided, and the xiphoid process is excised to expose the retrosternal space. Blunt finger dissection is carried cephalad, and the diaphragmatic pericardium is exposed and elevated with 2 clamps. After ensuring meticulous hemostasis to prevent false-positive results, the pericardium is incised between the clamps. The presence of blood or clot confirms tamponade or cardiac injury, prompting immediate conversion to median sternotomy for definitive exposure and repair. A negative window may be closed after confirming hemostasis, though some surgeons advocate leaving a drain in situ if the patient is unstable or suspicion remains high.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Cardiac Contusion
content: Myocardial contusion is the most common cardiac injury following blunt chest trauma, typically involving the right ventricle, given its anterior location. The pathophysiology involves direct myocardial compression between the sternum and spine, sudden deceleration forces, or a hydraulic effect from intravascular pressure surges. Clinically, these injuries can range from asymptomatic ECG changes to overt pump failure or arrhythmia. ECG may show sinus tachycardia, ST-T changes, pathologic Q waves, bundle branch blocks, atrioventricular nodal blocks, or premature ventricular contractions. [25] The phenomenon of commotio cordis—a lethal ventricular arrhythmia precipitated by blunt impact during cardiac repolarization—represents a nonstructural but fatal subset of cardiac contusion.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Cardiac Contusion
content: The aortic valve is the most frequently injured in blunt mediastinal trauma due to abrupt deceleration during early diastole when the valve is closed, and the transvalvular pressure gradient is maximal. [26] Myocardial contusion may be visualized on contrast-enhanced CT as focal or diffuse hypoenhancement or myocardial thickening with sharply demarcated borders, distinguishing it from infarction, which follows a vascular distribution and demonstrates indistinct margins. [27] Management is mainly supportive, focusing on volume resuscitation, inotropes or vasopressors as needed, and continuous cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia detection. Serial ECGs and troponin measurements are recommended. Patients with persistent hemodynamic or electrical instability should undergo formal echocardiography to evaluate for wall-motion abnormalities or pericardial effusion.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Myocardial Rupture
content: Myocardial rupture is a catastrophic complication of blunt cardiac trauma, often fatal before hospital arrival due to massive hemopericardium and tamponade. The right ventricle, being the most anterior and thinnest chamber, is most frequently affected. Rupture may also occur at the left atrial appendage, ventricular septum, or papillary muscles. In cases of ventricular septal rupture, presentation can be immediate or delayed, up to 48 hours postinjury, with initial ECG and troponin changes that mimic cardiac contusion. Clinical deterioration with new murmurs or heart failure should prompt emergent echocardiography to confirm the diagnosis.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Myocardial Rupture
content: Definitive management requires urgent cardiothoracic surgical repair under cardiopulmonary bypass. The approach is typically via median sternotomy, with direct closure of the defect using pledgeted 3-0 or 4-0 polypropylene sutures. Larger or friable defects may necessitate patch repair with autologous or synthetic material. Temporary stabilization with pericardial drainage and volume resuscitation may be attempted in the emergency setting while preparing for operative intervention.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Penetrating Cardiac Injury
content: Penetrating cardiac injuries, most often involving the right ventricle, carry high mortality but are potentially salvageable with rapid surgical intervention. Temporary control of bleeding can be achieved with skin staples, a Foley balloon tamponade, or direct digital pressure while preparing for definitive repair. Ventricular wounds should be repaired using running or interrupted horizontal mattress 3-0 polypropylene sutures on a tapered needle, often with Teflon pledgets to distribute tension and prevent suture pull-through. Sutures must be deep but not full-thickness, taking care to avoid coronary vessels. [25] [26] [27]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Penetrating Cardiac Injury
content: Atrial injuries can be managed with Satinsky or Allis clamps for temporary control and are typically closed using continuous or purse-string 3-0 polypropylene sutures extending approximately 5 mm beyond the wound margins. Pledgets are not routinely required but may be used in friable myocardium or left ventricular repairs where higher intramural pressures exist. After repair, the heart should be carefully palpated for thrills suggesting residual intracardiac communication, and the pericardium loosely reapproximated to prevent constriction.

content: Postoperative management includes continuous hemodynamic monitoring for arrhythmias, myocardial dysfunction, or bleeding. Complications such as mural thrombus, pericarditis, or ventricular aneurysm formation should be anticipated. Temporary epicardial pacing wires should be placed, particularly if conduction disturbances are present. Early and aggressive critical care coordination is crucial for optimizing cardiac recovery and preventing secondary complications.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Posttraumatic Pericarditis
content: Posttraumatic pericarditis is an uncommon but essential sequela of thoracic trauma, occurring even in patients without overt cardiac injury. This diagnosis can be challenging, as symptoms may be masked by coexisting traumatic injuries or nonspecific postoperative findings. The pathophysiology is thought to involve inflammation of the pericardium secondary to direct mechanical injury, hemopericardium, or sterile inflammatory response following cardiac contusion or pericardiotomy. Clinically, patients may present with pleuritic chest pain (often positional or relieved by leaning forward), pericardial friction rub, or evidence of diffuse ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression on ECG. Echocardiography may reveal a new or enlarging pericardial effusion, and though rare, tamponade physiology may develop, resulting in obstructive shock.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Posttraumatic Pericarditis
content: Treatment is mainly medical. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are first-line therapy for 1 to 2 weeks, while colchicine is recommended for up to 3 months to reduce recurrence and persistent inflammation, particularly in patients with contraindications to NSAIDs or renal impairment. [28] Corticosteroids should generally be avoided unless there is an autoimmune or uremic etiology, as they may delay healing and increase infection risk in trauma patients. Serial echocardiography is advised in cases with persistent symptoms or significant effusions to monitor for progression or constrictive physiology.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Great Vessel Injury
content: Injuries to the thoracic great vessels, including the aorta, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, superior vena cava, and innominate, carotid, and subclavian arteries, represent some of the most lethal forms of mediastinal trauma. Over 90% result from penetrating mechanisms, and approximately 80% of patients die at the scene due to exsanguination or rapid cardiovascular collapse. Survivors who reach the trauma bay require immediate recognition and precise operative planning. A distal upper extremity pulse does not exclude great vessel injury, as collateral circulation may mask arterial disruption.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Great Vessel Injury
content: In hemodynamically stable individuals, CTA is the diagnostic modality of choice, as it delineates the injury trajectory, vessel involvement, and the presence of active extravasation or a pseudoaneurysm. Operative approach depends on injury location: a median sternotomy for ascending aorta, innominate, and proximal carotid injuries; a left thoracotomy for descending aortic or left subclavian injuries; and a clamshell thoracotomy for extensive bilateral or central injuries. Precise incision selection is crucial for achieving proximal and distal vascular control, thereby minimizing operative time and blood loss. Endovascular stent-grafting may be considered in select cases with a contained hematoma or partial wall injury, particularly in the descending thoracic aorta.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Pulmonary Vessel Injury
content: Pulmonary artery and vein injuries are highly lethal, with mortality exceeding 70%, especially in central vessel involvement. Rapid hemorrhage control is paramount. In patients with exsanguinating bleeding, temporary hilar occlusion or twisting the pulmonary hilum can provide immediate control while definitive exposure is achieved. The intrapericardial pulmonary vessels are best approached via median sternotomy or clamshell thoracotomy for bilateral access.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Pulmonary Vessel Injury
content: The right pulmonary artery can be exposed by careful dissection between the superior vena cava and ascending aorta, taking care to avoid injury to adjacent structures. Anterior injuries may be amenable to primary repair with fine nonabsorbable sutures, while posterior injuries are often difficult to access and typically require cardiopulmonary bypass for safe and complete repair. [29] If a pulmonary vein must be ligated, a corresponding lobectomy or pneumonectomy should be performed to prevent venous congestion and infarction. [30] Postoperative management should focus on minimizing right ventricular strain, optimizing oxygenation, and monitoring for pulmonary edema and right heart failure.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Subclavian Vessel Injury
content: Subclavian artery and vein injuries are uncommon but carry significant morbidity due to their proximity to the brachial plexus, apex of the lung, and mediastinal structures. Fewer than 25% of patients present with “hard signs” of vascular injury (active hemorrhage, expanding hematoma, bruit, thrill, or distal ischemia). [30] [31] Massive hemorrhage from subclavian artery injury may necessitate rapid compression, resuscitative thoracotomy, or insertion of a balloon occlusion catheter for temporary hemostasis. Following revascularization, forearm fasciotomy should be considered to prevent compartment syndrome secondary to reperfusion.

Open repair remains necessary for complete transections, lacerations exceeding 50% of the vessel circumference, or complex injuries involving adjacent structures. Surgical exposure varies with laterality and segment: supraclavicular incision with possible extension into a median sternotomy for right-sided injuries, or anterolateral thoracotomy for left-sided or intrathoracic injuries. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, "Subclavian Artery Trauma," for further information.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Aortic Injury
content: Blunt traumatic aortic injury (BTAI) encompasses a spectrum of lesions ranging from minimal intimal disruptions to complete aortic transection, and remains one of the most lethal forms of thoracic trauma. The aortic isthmus, just distal to the left subclavian artery and tethered by the ligamentum arteriosum, is the most common site of injury due to its relative immobility during rapid deceleration. Mechanisms include restrained, front-impact moving vehicle collisions (MVC), high falls, and crush injuries. BTAI represents the second leading cause of death in blunt trauma, found in 20% to 25% of fatal MVCs at autopsy. [32]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Aortic Injury
content: Minimal aortic injury (MAI) accounts for 10% to 28% of all BTAIs and is considered a mild form, limited to the aortic intima. These lesions are increasingly recognized with high-resolution CTA. Radiographically, MAIs appear as small intimal irregularities or flaps less than 10 mm without external contour abnormality, corresponding to AAST grade I injury. Small pseudoaneurysms associated with limited intramural hematoma are classified as grade II injuries. [33] [34] [35] Aortic wall integrity is typically preserved, and these injuries heal spontaneously via reendothelialization. Management is nonoperative, emphasizing strict control of blood pressure and heart rate, with follow-up CTA at 48 to 72 hours post-injury and repeat imaging at 1 month to confirm resolution. [33] [34] [35]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Traumatic Aortic Rupture
content: Traumatic aortic rupture—also referred to as aortic transection—is a full-thickness tear of the aortic wall and represents a grade III (contained rupture ± pseudoaneurysm) or grade IV (free rupture) injury per the AAST classification. [35] These injuries are associated with massive mediastinal hemorrhage and rapid hemodynamic collapse, with prehospital mortality exceeding 90%. Among hospitalized individuals, mortality remains more than 30% even with definitive management. [32] Survivors often have contained ruptures stabilized by the adventitia or adjacent mediastinal tissues. Without intervention, most patients with grade III injuries will progress to complete rupture within 24 hours.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Traumatic Aortic Rupture
content: CXR may reveal indirect signs such as a widened mediastinum (>8 cm supine, >6 cm upright), loss of the aortopulmonary window, tracheal deviation to the right, depression of the left main bronchus, and abnormal aortic contour—all raising suspicion for aortic injury. [36] The definitive diagnosis is made via chest CTA, which provides a detailed anatomic assessment for surgical planning. Transesophageal echocardiography is a valuable adjunct in unstable patients or when CT is unavailable, offering high sensitivity and specificity for proximal aortic lesions. However, visualization of the distal ascending and arch segments may be limited by air artifact. [37]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Traumatic Aortic Rupture
content: Initial management of all suspected aortic injuries focuses on anti-impulse therapy—reducing aortic wall stress to prevent extension or rupture. Beta-blockade, typically with IV esmolol, is first-line therapy due to its rapid onset and short half-life, targeting heart rates below 100 bpm and systolic blood pressure below 100 mm Hg. If beta-blockers are contraindicated, diltiazem may be substituted. For persistent hypertension, IV nitroglycerin or nitroprusside can be added once adequate beta-blockade is achieved. [38] Patients should be stabilized hemodynamically and have other life-threatening injuries addressed before definitive aortic repair.

[39] [40] TEVAR is best suited for grade II through III injuries with suitable anatomy and absence of arch involvement.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Traumatic Aortic Rupture
content: Open surgical repair, typically via left posterolateral thoracotomy or median sternotomy, remains indicated for grade IV injuries, arch involvement, or cases unsuitable for endovascular repair. The procedure generally involves resection of the disrupted segment and interposition grafting with a synthetic conduit, often requiring left heart bypass or partial cardiopulmonary bypass for distal perfusion. Complications include spinal cord ischemia, phrenic nerve injury, coronary vessel compromise, and prolonged ischemic time. Postoperatively, patients require intensive blood pressure control, neurologic monitoring, and serial imaging to assess for endoleak, graft migration, or pseudoaneurysm formation. Early recognition, multidisciplinary coordination, and precise surgical technique remain critical to improving survival and long-term outcomes following traumatic aortic injury.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Esophageal Injury
content: Esophageal trauma, though uncommon, carries one of the highest morbidity and mortality rates among thoracic injuries due to diagnostic delays and the esophagus’s inherent fragility. In the US, gunshot wounds account for 70% to 80% of penetrating esophageal trauma, stab injuries for 15% to 20%, and blunt mechanisms for only 1% to 13% of cases, as the esophagus is relatively protected from deceleration forces. [41] [42] The absence of a serosal layer and the segmental, tenuous blood supply hinder healing and increase the risk of dehiscence following repair. Furthermore, a negative thoracoabdominal pressure gradient promotes reflux and facilitates translocation of enteric contents through the injury, thereby predisposing the patient to mediastinitis, empyema, and sepsis. Clinically, symptoms may be subtle and nonspecific, including retrosternal chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, the Hamman sign (a mediastinal crunch), fever, vomiting, dyspnea, dysphagia, or odynophagia, and are often delayed, underscoring the need for a high index of suspicion. [41]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Esophageal Injury
content: In hemodynamically stable individuals, diagnosis can be achieved using contrast esophagography, initially with water-soluble contrast to avoid mediastinal contamination, followed by barium if no leak is visualized to increase sensitivity for small mucosal disruptions. A chest CT scan with oral contrast can complement these studies, delineating mediastinal air, fluid collections, or extraluminal contrast suggestive of perforation.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Esophageal Injury
content: Management centers on prompt source control, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and nutritional support. Early surgical exploration and repair are generally indicated, given the high mortality associated with delayed treatment. The approach depends on the location of the injury: Cervical esophagus → left neck incision, allowing protection of the recurrent laryngeal nerve Thoracic esophagus → right posterolateral thoracotomy, exposing the esophagus adjacent to the descending aorta Distal esophagus → transabdominal approach via laparotomy

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Esophageal Injury
content: At surgery, the full extent of the injury is assessed using proximal and distal linear myotomies. When feasible, a 2-layer primary repair is performed—absorbable sutures for the mucosa and nonabsorbable sutures for the muscularis—often over a bougie or esophagoscope to maintain luminal patency. The repair is buttressed with viable tissue such as pleura, pericardial fat, or an intercostal muscle flap, and the mediastinum and pleural spaces are copiously irrigated and widely drained. In cases where repair is not possible due to extensive tissue destruction or instability, controlled external drainage or esophageal diversion with a T-tube may be used for source control.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Esophageal Injury
content: Endoscopic options such as covered stent placement can be considered for select contained injuries or as adjuncts following surgical washout. However, these carry risks of migration, bronchial compression, and dislodgment during manipulation. Postoperative care involves continued antibiotics, enteral or parenteral nutrition, and close monitoring for complications, including mediastinal abscess, empyema, leak (30%–40%), stricture formation, and esophageal dysmotility. [45] Early recognition, multidisciplinary coordination, and meticulous operative technique remain vital in improving survival in patients with esophageal trauma. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, "Esophageal Trauma," for further information.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Tracheobronchial Injury
content: Tracheobronchial injuries, though rare, represent one of the most lethal forms of mediastinal trauma due to their association with massive air leaks, tension pneumothorax, and respiratory compromise. The intrathoracic trachea lies in the midline with slight rightward deviation secondary to the aortic arch. The carina bifurcates at approximately the T4 vertebral level, and most traumatic injuries occur within 2.5 cm of the carina; the right main bronchus is affected more frequently than the left due to its shorter course and reduced anatomic protection. [46] The distal trachea and right lower bronchus are therefore the most commonly injured sites.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Tracheobronchial Injury
content: Tracheobronchial injury occurs in approximately 1% to 3% of blunt chest trauma and 2% to 9% of penetrating trauma, though 30% to 80% of patients succumb before hospital arrival. [47] Up to 20% of cases involve concomitant esophageal rupture, increasing mortality risk. [48] Mechanisms in blunt injury include a sudden rise in intraluminal pressure against a closed glottis during anteroposterior chest compression, hyperextension of the neck, and shearing forces between the fixed cricoid cartilage and carina during rapid deceleration. These mechanisms often result in membranous tracheal ruptures or circumferential tears at points of fixation.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Tracheobronchial Injury
content: Symptoms overlap with those of esophageal or pulmonary injury and may include hoarseness, hemoptysis, respiratory distress, pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, or subcutaneous emphysema. A persistent air leak despite adequate chest tube placement should raise suspicion of a tracheobronchial disruption. Flexible bronchoscopy remains the gold standard for diagnosis, allowing direct visualization, assessment of injury extent, and airway control.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Tracheobronchial Injury
content: Airway stabilization is the critical first step. Awake fiberoptic intubation with the endotracheal tube passed distal to the defect (if feasible) minimizes further disruption. In large or complex lacerations where visualization is obscured by blood or secretions, rigid bronchoscopy may provide better control and visualization. However, it requires posterior head extension and should therefore be avoided until a cervical spine injury is excluded. title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Tracheobronchial Injury
content: Once the defect is identified, devitalized tissue should be sharply debrided to viable margins. Tension-free primary repair with interrupted absorbable sutures (eg, 4-0 or 5-0 polydioxanone or Vicryl) is preferred. Circumferential injuries may necessitate segmental resection with end-to-end anastomosis. In cervical repairs, postoperative neck flexion should be maintained (eg, chin-to-chest suturing or a flexion collar) to reduce anastomotic tension. To further minimize tension, pretracheal plane dissection can allow limited mobilization, while suprahyoid or infrahyoid release may be used in cases requiring additional length. [16] [51] Overzealous mobilization, however, risks devascularization, which can lead to anastomotic dehiscence or late stricture formation. Potential complications include granulation tissue formation and fibrotic stenosis, anastomotic leak, mediastinitis, or chronic airway obstruction. Long-term follow-up with surveillance bronchoscopy and, when indicated, balloon dilation or stenting is recommended to manage late airway narrowing.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Thoracic Duct Injury
content: The thoracic duct originates from the cisterna chyli at approximately the L2 vertebral level, ascends through the posterior mediastinum on the right side of the thoracic aorta between the azygos vein and the esophagus, and crosses to the left at the T4–T5 level, coursing posterior to the aortic arch before terminating at the left venous angle, where the left subclavian and internal jugular veins meet. Disruption can occur through blunt hyperflexion or hyperextension injuries of the thoracic spine that shear or stretch lymphatic channels, or during penetrating or iatrogenic trauma involving the posterior mediastinum, esophagectomy, or cardiothoracic surgery.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Thoracic Duct Injury
content: Diagnosis is confirmed by the appearance of milky or opalescent fluid draining from a chest tube or wound, with laboratory analysis demonstrating triglyceride levels of 110 mg/dL or more and lymphocytic predominance, consistent with chylothorax. [52] [53] Conservative management is first-line and consists of adequate pleural drainage, bowel rest or a low-fat diet, restriction of long-chain triglycerides, and supplementation with medium-chain triglycerides to reduce lymphatic flow. Octreotide (100–200 µg subcutaneously every 8 hours) or a continuous somatostatin infusion can be used to reduce lymphatic secretion. Patients who continue to have high-output drainage (>1 L/day) or persistent chyle leak after resuming an oral diet should be transitioned to total parenteral nutrition without lipids to minimize lymphatic flow.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Thoracic Duct Injury
content: If conservative management fails after 2 to 3 weeks, interventional radiologic embolization of the thoracic duct following intranodal lymphangiography offers a minimally invasive option with high success rates. Surgical intervention is indicated for persistent high-output chyle leaks or for cases in which nonoperative management fails. Surgical ligation of the thoracic duct is most effectively performed at the right inferior mediastinum, typically between the aortic hiatus and the azygos vein, just above the diaphragm. [52] [53] Complications of untreated or chronic chyle leak include malnutrition, hypoproteinemia, electrolyte disturbances, respiratory compromise, and immunosuppression from lymphocyte loss.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Sternal Fractures
content: Sternal fractures occur in approximately 8% of blunt thoracic trauma cases and up to 18% of polytrauma involving thoracic injuries, commonly resulting from direct anterior chest compression during MVCs (especially with seatbelt or airbag deployment) or high-energy deceleration injuries. [54] They are frequently associated with rib fractures, pulmonary contusion, flail chest, cardiac contusion, cardiac tamponade, pneumothorax, and blunt aortic injury, and thus warrant a high index of suspicion for concomitant mediastinal trauma. In cases of isolated, nondisplaced sternal fractures, management is typically conservative, focusing on analgesia, respiratory support, and short-term observation (minimum 24 hours) to monitor for blunt cardiac injury, which may present with ECG abnormalities or elevated troponins. Most isolated fractures heal spontaneously with minimal complications, and patients generally experience full recovery within 10 to 12 weeks. [54]

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Treatment / Management -- Sternal Fractures
content: Operative intervention is reserved for displaced, unstable, or comminuted fractures that impair chest wall mechanics, result in respiratory compromise, or cause severe pain refractory to conservative therapy. Surgical fixation can be performed using stainless steel wires, sternal plating systems, or rigid fixation with plates and screws, which provide superior stability and pain relief, facilitating earlier mobilization and improved pulmonary function. [55] Postoperatively, patients should be monitored for infection, nonunion, or hardware migration, though complication rates are low with modern osteosynthesis techniques. Overall, sternal fractures serve as an essential marker of high-energy chest trauma, requiring a thorough assessment for associated cardiac and mediastinal injuries. Still, when isolated, they generally carry an excellent prognosis.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis of mediastinal trauma depends on several factors, including the type and severity of trauma (blunt versus penetrating), the structures involved, associated injuries, timing of diagnosis and treatment, and the patient’s age and overall condition. Because the mediastinum contains vital organs such as the heart, great vessels, trachea, and esophagus, injury to any of these structures can result in rapid hemodynamic compromise and high mortality if not promptly recognized and managed. Many mediastinal injuries occur in the setting of polytrauma, and the prognosis worsens significantly when there are concomitant traumatic brain injuries, abdominal injuries, or multiple system involvement. Poor prognostic indicators include traumatic cardiac arrest, delayed presentation (>24 hours), persistent hypotension, neurologic deficits suggesting spinal or cerebral injury, and signs of sepsis.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Prognosis
content: Blunt mediastinal trauma, often caused by high-velocity MVCs or deceleration injuries, carries a mortality rate exceeding 30% to 50% when major vascular or cardiac structures are involved. However, isolated injuries such as sternal fractures or small venous tears typically have an excellent outcome with conservative management. In contrast, penetrating mediastinal trauma has mortality rates approaching 80% to 90% when the heart or great vessels are injured. Still, outcomes improve substantially when patients arrive hemodynamically stable and undergo rapid surgical exploration and repair.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Prognosis
content: Advances in prehospital care, trauma imaging (especially CT angiography, or CTA), and endovascular and surgical techniques have significantly improved early detection and survival rates for many patients. Contained vascular injuries, minor tracheobronchial disruptions, and isolated esophageal tears generally have good outcomes if diagnosed early and treated appropriately, while delayed diagnosis of esophageal perforation or persistent chylothorax can lead to sepsis, malnutrition, and multiorgan failure. Ultimately, the best outcomes depend on early recognition, rapid resuscitation, and coordinated multidisciplinary management involving trauma surgeons, thoracic surgeons, intensivists, and radiologists—emphasizing that timely intervention and integrated critical care are the strongest determinants of survival in mediastinal trauma.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Deterrence and patient education for mediastinal trauma center on both preventing high-risk mechanisms of injury and educating patients about early recognition of complications following thoracic trauma. Mediastinal trauma most often results from MVCs, falls, and acts of violence, making targeted safety education essential. Wearing seatbelts, obeying speed limits, avoiding driving under the influence, and ensuring proper child restraints are among the most effective traffic safety measures to prevent blunt trauma to the thorax.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Likewise, injury prevention for falls should include practicing ladder safety (extending at least 3 feet above the landing surface, not standing on the top 3 rungs, maintaining 3 points of contact, and using a buddy system), recognizing personal fall risks such as medication adverse effects or environmental hazards, wearing nonslip footwear, setting realistic exertion goals, and adhering to workplace safety protocols, especially in industrial settings with heavy machinery or impalement risks. Firearm safety is another key aspect of prevention: all guns should be stored unloaded and locked, with ammunition kept separately, and safes or trigger locks used to secure them. Additionally, keys should be kept out of the reach of children and unauthorized individuals. Firearms should always be handled responsibly—pointed in a safe direction, with fingers off the trigger until ready to fire, and never left unattended.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: From a clinical standpoint, patient education following thoracic trauma should emphasize awareness of delayed complications such as esophageal leaks, tracheobronchial stenosis, pericarditis, or chylothorax, which can develop days or weeks after injury. Patients should be instructed to seek immediate medical care for new or worsening chest pain, dyspnea, hoarseness, hemoptysis, or fever. Education on smoking cessation, pulmonary hygiene, and rehabilitation helps optimize recovery and prevent secondary pulmonary complications. Interprofessional collaboration among trauma surgeons, primary care clinicians, nurses, respiratory and physical therapists is critical to ensuring coordinated follow-up, reinforcing safety behaviors, and promoting a patient-centered recovery. Overall, effective deterrence and education require both community-level prevention strategies and personalized posttrauma education, aiming to reduce the incidence, severity, and long-term morbidity associated with mediastinal trauma.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Pearls and other issues include the following: Patients with mediastinal trauma should be evaluated using the ATLS protocol. Endoscopic diagnostic tests are helpful in those with trauma with cardiopulmonary collapse; they can aid in the identification of mediastinal injuries, can be used to stop hemorrhage, and/or can help plan the surgical approach. Patients with mediastinal injury, especially from blunt trauma, will often have multiple injuries and may have nonspecific signs and symptoms; therefore, it is crucial to assess all mediastinal organs for injury using imaging studies. Patients with penetrating mediastinal trauma have the highest survival rate among all patients undergoing resuscitative thoracotomy. When proceeding to the operating room, consideration should be given to having a cell-saver available for potential large-volume blood loss, bypass available for cardiac and aortic injuries, and appropriate shunts and damage-control products as needed.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective management of mediastinal trauma demands a highly coordinated, multidisciplinary approach that emphasizes rapid assessment, decisive intervention, and seamless communication across the care team. Physicians and advanced clinicians play key roles in the early recognition and prioritization of life-threatening injuries, guiding resuscitation efforts, and determining the need for surgical exploration or transfer to a higher level of care. Trauma surgeons, cardiothoracic surgeons, and emergency clinicians must collaborate closely to integrate diagnostic imaging, hemodynamic monitoring, and operative planning. Nurses provide continuous bedside assessment, manage invasive lines and chest tubes, and communicate subtle clinical changes that may indicate deterioration. Pharmacists contribute to the timely delivery of blood products, analgesics, and antimicrobials, and to monitoring for drug interactions, as well as to optimizing pain control and sedation strategies. Respiratory therapists play a crucial role in airway management and ventilatory support, particularly in patients with tracheobronchial injuries or pulmonary compromise.

Respiratory therapists play a crucial role in airway management and ventilatory support, particularly in patients with tracheobronchial injuries or pulmonary compromise.

title: Mediastinal Trauma -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Optimizing patient-centered care and safety in mediastinal trauma hinges on clear, structured interprofessional communication—particularly through trauma huddles, handoff protocols, and standardized documentation. Strategies such as massive transfusion protocols, damage control principles, and multidisciplinary rounds enhance coordination and ensure that all team members understand evolving priorities. Collaboration with rehabilitation specialists and social workers supports holistic recovery and reintegration after acute stabilization. Ongoing simulation training, debriefings, and performance reviews strengthen team performance, reduce medical errors, and improve patient outcomes. Ultimately, integrating technical expertise with open communication and mutual respect among all health professionals fosters a culture of safety and continuous improvement in the complex care of patients with mediastinal trauma.
